Lab 12: Who Counts, and How

84-355 Democracy’s Data | Week 12

Your name here

August 06, 2026

Before we start

The Constitution orders a count. Article I requires an “actual Enumeration” every ten years, and everything downstream — how many seats your state gets, how districts are drawn, where §203 language assistance is required — runs off that number.

But a count requires categories, and categories are made by people. James Scott’s argument, which you read for Tuesday, is that states must simplify in order to govern: to administer a population you first have to render it legible, and the rendering is never neutral. Today you will hold the instrument that does the rendering for American democracy.

The file is called P.L. 94-171. A 1975 statute requires the Census Bureau to deliver it to every state within a year of Census Day, specifically so that legislatures can draw districts. It is the legal foundation of every redistricting cycle, including the ones you will study in Weeks 14 and 15.

Everything is base R. Work in order.

Part 1: The file the law requires

d <- read.csv("data/pl94171_counties.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
              colClasses = c(fips = "character"))
dim(d)
#> [1] 503  27
table(d$state)
#> 
#>       Hawaii  Mississippi   New Mexico     New York Pennsylvania        Texas 
#>            5           82           33           62           67          254

Six states, 503 counties. Start at home:

a <- d[d$fips == "42003", ]
a[, c("county", "state", "total", "white", "black", "asian", "two_or_more")]
#>               county        state   total  white  black asian two_or_more
#> 184 Allegheny County Pennsylvania 1250578 946321 163678 58541       65706

Allegheny County had 1,250,578 people on 1 April 2020. That is not an estimate and not a projection; it is the number the Census Bureau certified, and Pennsylvania’s districts were drawn from it.

Part 2: The first question — race

Table P1 asks one question and produces seventy-one columns. We have kept the main ones:

a[, c("total", "one_race", "white", "black", "aian", "asian", "nhpi",
      "other_race", "two_or_more")]
#>       total one_race  white  black aian asian nhpi other_race two_or_more
#> 184 1250578  1184872 946321 163678 1909 58541  357      14066       65706

The seven “alone” categories plus everyone reporting two or more races. It has to add up, and it does:

with(a, one_race + two_or_more == total)
#> [1] TRUE

The full table goes further than this. Because a person may check any combination of six race boxes, the Census publishes 63 distinct race categories — every combination, from “White alone” through “White; Black; American Indian; Asian; Pacific Islander; Some Other Race.” That is what the other sixty columns hold.

Sixty-three categories is not the Census Bureau being fussy. It is what happens when you take an idea that people experience as simple and try to make it administrable.

Part 3: The second question

Here is the thing that catches everyone out. The Census does not treat Hispanic or Latino origin as a race. It is a separate question, asked separately, and a Hispanic respondent also answers the race question.

So there are two different ways to ask how white a place is.

st <- aggregate(cbind(total, white, nh_white, hispanic) ~ state,
                data = d, FUN = sum)
st$white_pct   <- round(100 * st$white / st$total, 1)
st$nhwhite_pct <- round(100 * st$nh_white / st$total, 1)
st$gap         <- round(st$white_pct - st$nhwhite_pct, 1)

st[order(-st$gap), c("state", "total", "white_pct", "nhwhite_pct", "gap")]
#>          state    total white_pct nhwhite_pct  gap
#> 3   New Mexico  2117522      51.0        36.5 14.5
#> 6        Texas 29145505      50.1        39.7 10.4
#> 4     New York 20201249      55.2        52.5  2.7
#> 5 Pennsylvania 13002700      75.0        73.5  1.5
#> 1       Hawaii  1455271      22.9        21.6  1.3
#> 2  Mississippi  2961279      56.0        55.4  0.6
s <- st[order(st$white_pct), ]
par(mar = c(5, 10, 4, 2))
bp <- barplot(rbind(s$nhwhite_pct, s$white_pct - s$nhwhite_pct),
        horiz = TRUE, las = 1, names.arg = s$state, beside = FALSE,
        col = c("#2166AC", "#92C5DE"), border = NA, xlim = c(0, 80),
        xlab = "% white", main = "Two answers to the same question")
legend("bottomright", c("Non-Hispanic white", "Hispanic and white"),
       fill = c("#2166AC", "#92C5DE"), border = NA, bty = "n", cex = 0.85)

New Mexico is 51.0% white by the race question and 36.5% white once you account for the ethnicity question — a gap of 14.5 points.

By one measure New Mexico is a majority-white state. By the other it is not close. Both numbers are correct. They are answers to different questions, and almost nobody reporting a figure like this tells you which one they used.

Texas shows the same thing at 10.4 points. Mississippi shows almost none (0.6), because very few Mississippians are both Hispanic and white.

The gap is not a flaw in the data. It is the visible seam between two ways of classifying people that the United States has never fully reconciled.

Part 4: “None of these”

Look at the other_race column — people who answered the race question by rejecting every box offered.

st2 <- aggregate(cbind(total, other_race, two_or_more) ~ state, data = d, FUN = sum)
st2$other_pct <- round(100 * st2$other_race / st2$total, 1)
st2$two_pct   <- round(100 * st2$two_or_more / st2$total, 1)
st2[order(-st2$other_pct), c("state", "other_pct", "two_pct")]
#>          state other_pct two_pct
#> 3   New Mexico      15.0    19.9
#> 6        Texas      13.6    17.6
#> 4     New York      10.9     8.7
#> 5 Pennsylvania       3.9     6.0
#> 2  Mississippi       1.9     3.7
#> 1       Hawaii       1.8    25.3

Fifteen percent of New Mexicans, and 13.6% of Texans, looked at the race question and chose “Some Other Race.”

Who are they? The file answers this directly, because it reports each race crossed with Hispanic origin.

tot_other  <- sum(d$other_race)
nh_other   <- sum(d$nh_other)
hisp_other <- tot_other - nh_other

cat("Chose 'Some Other Race':", format(tot_other, big.mark = ","), "people
")
#> Chose 'Some Other Race': 7,072,769 people
cat("  Hispanic:    ", format(hisp_other, big.mark = ","),
    sprintf("(%.1f%%)
", 100 * hisp_other / tot_other))
#>   Hispanic:     6,684,740 (94.5%)
cat("  non-Hispanic:", format(nh_other, big.mark = ","),
    sprintf("(%.1f%%)
", 100 * nh_other / tot_other))
#>   non-Hispanic: 388,029 (5.5%)

94.5% of the people who rejected every race box are Hispanic.

Read that again, because it is the finding of this lab. The residual category on the race question — the box for people who fit nowhere else — is, in practice, an ethnicity box. Seven million people were asked their race, found that the form did not offer one they recognised, and the overwhelming majority of them were the same seven million the next question was about.

The form asks a question a large minority of respondents do not think is well posed, and then records their refusal as if it were an answer.

And the multiracial column varies enormously — 25.3% in Hawaii against 3.7% in Mississippi. Some of that is real difference in who lives where. Some of it is that the 2020 form invited people to elaborate in ways the 2010 form did not, and millions of people answered differently to a question about themselves that had not changed.

Part 5: Counted where you sleep

The Census counts people at their “usual residence” — where they sleep most of the time. For most people that is uncontroversial. For some it is not.

d$corr_pct <- round(100 * d$gq_correctional / d$total, 1)
head(d[order(-d$corr_pct),
       c("county", "state", "total", "gq_correctional", "corr_pct")], 8)
#>               county        state total gq_correctional corr_pct
#> 209    Forest County Pennsylvania  6973            2653     38.0
#> 33  Issaquena County  Mississippi  1338             493     36.8
#> 364  Hudspeth County        Texas  3202             996     31.1
#> 297    Concho County        Texas  3303            1012     30.6
#> 334     Garza County        Texas  5816            1731     29.8
#> 376     Jones County        Texas 19663            5073     25.8
#> 417  Mitchell County        Texas  8990            2113     23.5
#> 262       Bee County        Texas 31047            7242     23.3

Thirty-eight percent of Forest County, Pennsylvania is in a state correctional facility. 2,653 people out of 6,973.

Those 2,653 people cannot vote in Pennsylvania. They are counted as residents of Forest County for the purpose of drawing districts, and they are represented by a legislator they had no part in choosing — while the communities they came from, mostly urban, lose the population that would have counted toward their own representation.

This is what “prison gerrymandering” means, and it is a consequence of a residence rule rather than of anybody drawing a map badly. Some states now reallocate incarcerated people to their home addresses before redistricting. Pennsylvania began doing so in 2021.

The same rule catches students:

d$coll_pct <- round(100 * d$gq_college / d$total, 1)
head(d[order(-d$coll_pct),
       c("county", "state", "total", "gq_college", "coll_pct")], 5)
#>               county        state  total gq_college coll_pct
#> 175  Tompkins County     New York 105740      13084     12.4
#> 16  Claiborne County  Mississippi   9135       1005     11.0
#> 486    Waller County        Texas  56794       5814     10.2
#> 58  Oktibbeha County  Mississippi  51788       5160     10.0
#> 196    Centre County Pennsylvania 158172      14269      9.0

Centre County is 9.0% dormitory. Tompkins County, New York — Cornell — is 12.4%. On 1 April 2020 those students were mostly not there, because of the pandemic, and the Bureau had to decide what to do about it.

Part 6: What this file will not tell you

The numbers have noise in them, on purpose. For 2020 the Census Bureau applied differential privacy: small random adjustments designed so that no individual’s answers can be reconstructed from published tables. State totals are untouched and county figures are close, but the smaller the geography the more the injected noise matters — and districts are drawn from blocks, not counties. Whether the protection was worth the distortion was litigated by states, and remains contested.

The categories are not stable. Every decade the race question changes, and comparisons across decades compare instruments as much as populations. The 2030 question is expected to change again, most likely by combining race and Hispanic origin into one question — which would erase, at a stroke, the gap you measured in Part 3.

A count is not a census of citizens. P.L. 94-171 counts residents. That is what apportionment uses, and attempts to change it have failed in court so far.

Part 7: On your own

This is the part you turn in. You are not being asked to write code. Each option is a working chunk with one thing to change.

Pick one.

Option A — The gap, county by county

this_state <- "Texas"          # <- change to any state in the data

s <- d[d$state == this_state, ]
s$white_pct   <- 100 * s$white / s$total
s$nhwhite_pct <- 100 * s$nh_white / s$total
s$gap <- s$white_pct - s$nhwhite_pct

plot(s$white_pct, s$nhwhite_pct, pch = 19, col = "#2166AC88", cex = 1.2,
     xlim = c(0, 100), ylim = c(0, 100),
     xlab = "% white (race question only)",
     ylab = "% non-Hispanic white (both questions)",
     main = paste("Two measures of white population:", this_state))
abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "grey50")

big <- head(s[order(-s$gap), ], 6)
big[, c("county", "total", "white_pct", "nhwhite_pct", "gap")]
#>               county total white_pct nhwhite_pct      gap
#> 444    Reeves County 14748  54.73963   11.506645 43.23298
#> 503    Zavala County  9670  47.54912    5.915202 41.63392
#> 315     Duval County  9831  50.79849    9.531075 41.26742
#> 373  Jim Hogg County  4838  48.22241    8.557255 39.66515
#> 374 Jim Wells County 38891  57.04919   17.903885 39.14530
#> 334     Garza County  5816  74.36382   37.173315 37.19051

Write about: every point sits below the diagonal, and the vertical distance is the gap. Which counties have the largest gaps, and what do they have in common? Then the question that matters for this course: a news story reports that a county is “60% white.” Depending on which measure was used, that same county might be 60% or 35%. Which measure would you want a redistricting case to use, and does the answer depend on what the case is about?

Option B — Who is warehoused where

kind <- "gq_correctional"      # <- try gq_college, gq_nursing, gq_military

d$share <- 100 * d[[kind]] / d$total
top <- head(d[order(-d$share), ], 12)
top <- top[order(top$share), ]

par(mar = c(5, 13, 4, 2))
barplot(top$share, names.arg = paste0(sub(" County","",top$county), ", ",
        substr(top$state, 1, 2)), horiz = TRUE, las = 1,
        col = "#B2182B", border = NA, xlab = "% of county population",
        main = paste("Group quarters:", sub("gq_", "", kind)))

top[order(-top$share), c("county", "state", "total", kind, "share")]
#>               county        state total gq_correctional    share
#> 209    Forest County Pennsylvania  6973            2653 38.04675
#> 33  Issaquena County  Mississippi  1338             493 36.84604
#> 364  Hudspeth County        Texas  3202             996 31.10556
#> 297    Concho County        Texas  3303            1012 30.63881
#> 334     Garza County        Texas  5816            1731 29.76272
#> 376     Jones County        Texas 19663            5073 25.79973
#> 417  Mitchell County        Texas  8990            2113 23.50389
#> 262       Bee County        Texas 31047            7242 23.32593
#> 250  Anderson County        Texas 57922           13344 23.03788
#> 444    Reeves County        Texas 14748            2981 20.21291
#> 388  La Salle County        Texas  6664            1338 20.07803
#> 377    Karnes County        Texas 14710            2929 19.91162

Write about: describe the counties at the top. Are they large or small, and why does that matter for the percentage? Then take the representation question seriously. For prisons, the people counted cannot vote where they are counted. For colleges, they mostly can. For nursing homes, they can. Does the objection to prison gerrymandering rest on the counting, or on the disenfranchisement? If Pennsylvania restored the vote to incarcerated people tomorrow, would the problem go away?

Option C — How much does the question shape the answer?

metrics <- data.frame(
  state = st$state,
  race_question_white = st$white_pct,
  both_questions_white = st$nhwhite_pct,
  hispanic_pct = round(100 * st$hispanic / st$total, 1))
metrics$ratio <- round(metrics$race_question_white /
                       metrics$both_questions_white, 2)
metrics[order(-metrics$ratio), ]
#>          state race_question_white both_questions_white hispanic_pct ratio
#> 3   New Mexico                51.0                 36.5         47.7  1.40
#> 6        Texas                50.1                 39.7         39.3  1.26
#> 1       Hawaii                22.9                 21.6          9.5  1.06
#> 4     New York                55.2                 52.5         19.5  1.05
#> 5 Pennsylvania                75.0                 73.5          8.1  1.02
#> 2  Mississippi                56.0                 55.4          3.6  1.01
# Is the gap just a function of how Hispanic a state is?
round(cor(metrics$hispanic_pct,
          metrics$race_question_white - metrics$both_questions_white), 3)
#> [1] 0.982

Write about: the gap is strongly related to how Hispanic a state is — which is unsurprising, since the gap is by construction the Hispanic-and-white population. The interesting part is the ratio column: in New Mexico the race question inflates the white share by a factor of 1.40. Then push further: Hawaii has a small gap but the lowest white share of any state here, and a quarter of its people report two or more races. Does the race question serve Hawaii well? A good answer says what a better question would look like and what it would cost.

Option D — Ask your own question

Look up your home county. Compare Mississippi’s counties to Hawaii’s. Find the county with the largest multiracial share and work out why.

What to submit. Knit to HTML or PDF and upload to Canvas, with your chosen chunk and two or three paragraphs of interpretation.

The writing is the assignment. I am not grading your code — it is my code. I am grading whether you can look at an official count and see the decisions inside it.

Where the data came from

U.S. Census Bureau, 2020 Census Redistricting Data (P.L. 94-171) Summary File, legacy format (https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/decennial/2020/data/01-Redistricting_File--PL_94-171/), for Pennsylvania, Texas, New York, Hawaii, Mississippi and New Mexico. Tables P1 (race), P2 (Hispanic or Latino origin by race) and P5 (group quarters).

Six states rather than fifty, because each state ships about 300 MB and these six pull the race and ethnicity questions apart in usefully different directions.

County names are joined from the Census Gazetteer rather than the file’s own geographic header, which populates the name field inconsistently — Pennsylvania carries “Allegheny County” and Hawaii leaves it blank. That is a small example of the thing this whole course keeps finding: even an authoritative file needs checking before you trust a column.

On the design of this lab. The structure — race, then ethnicity as a second dimension, then the question of what the categories do — follows Moon Duchin’s PUBPOL 2130 at Cornell, Data and the State, adapted from Python to R. The readings for Tuesday (Scott, and Nobles on race and censuses) are hers as well.

The script that downloaded, parsed and checked these files is data/build-data.R. It verifies that P1 and P2 each decompose exactly, and that Allegheny County’s total matches the published figure, before writing anything.
